facts.statement: The type species of the genus Giraffatitan is G. brancai.
facts.quote: type_species: Giraffatitan brancai

facts.statement: Giraffatitan brancai was originally classified as the species Brachiosaurus brancai.
facts.quote: synonyms: Brachiosaurus brancai

facts.statement: The genus Giraffatitan was established by Paul in 1988.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan fossils date to the Late Jurassic period, specifically the Tithonian stage.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Jurassic (Tithonian),

facts.statement: Giraffatitan lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic in what is now the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
facts.quote: lived during the late Jurassic Period (Kimmeridgian–Tithonian stages) in what is now Lindi Region, Tanzania

facts.statement: The species G. brancai was named in honor of Wilhelm von Branca, who led the expedition that found the fossils in the Tendaguru Formation.
facts.quote: named in honor of German paleontologist Wilhelm von Branca, who was a driving force behind the expedition that discovered it in the Tendaguru Formation

facts.statement: Werner Janensch originally described Giraffatitan brancai as Brachiosaurus brancai from the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan brancai was originally described by German paleontologist Werner Janensch as a species of the North American sauropod Brachiosaurus from the Morrison Formation, as Brachiosaurus brancai

facts.statement: Recent research indicates that the Tendaguru material differs so significantly from the type species of Brachiosaurus that it warrants its own genus.
facts.quote: Recent research shows that the differences between the type species of Brachiosaurus and the Tendaguru material are so large that the African material should be placed in a separate genus

facts.statement: Giraffatitan was once considered the largest dinosaur, but this record has been surpassed by larger titanosaurians.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was for many decades known as the largest dinosaur but recent discoveries of several larger dinosaurs prove otherwise

facts.statement: Specimen HMN XV2, with a fibula 13% larger than that of HMN SII, is estimated to have been 23 to 26 meters long and weighed 40 to 48 metric tons.
facts.quote: specimen HMN XV2, represented by a fibula 13% larger than the corresponding material on HMN SII, would have measured around 23 - 26 m long and weighed about 40 - 48 MT

facts.statement: In 1906, mining engineer Bernhard Wilhelm Sattler discovered an enormous bone at Tendaguru near Lindi in German East Africa (now Tanzania).
facts.quote: In 1906, mining engineer Bernhard Wilhelm Sattler, while travelling, noticed an enormous bone jutting out of the ground at the Tendaguru (the "steep hill") near Lindi, in what was then German East Africa, today Lindi Region, Tanzania

facts.statement: Werner Janensch and Edwin Hennig arrived in Dar es Salaam on April 2, 1909.
facts.quote: Both men arrived in Dar es Salaam on 2 April 1909

facts.statement: Between 1909 and 1912, the Tendaguru expedition opened approximately one hundred paleontological quarries.
facts.quote: During four field seasons, of 1909, 1910, 1911 and 1912, about a hundred paleontological quarries were opened

facts.statement: The first quarry containing Giraffatitan material, Site D, was opened on June 21, 1909.
facts.quote: The first quarry with Giraffatitan material was "Site D", located about 1 km northeast of the Tendaguru Hill and opened on 21 June 1909

facts.statement: Site S, located one kilometer southwest of Tendaguru Hill, was the most important source of Giraffatitan fossils.
facts.quote: The most important source of Giraffatitan fossils would be "Site S" at one kilometre southwest of the hill

facts.statement: Werner Janensch later realized that the Site S excavation had yielded two skeletons.
facts.quote: Only much later Janensch realised that two skeletons had been present

facts.statement: Skelett SII was the larger of the two skeletons found at Site S, but it was still a subadult.
facts.quote: Skelett SII was larger but despite its size still a subadult individual

facts.statement: The Tendaguru expedition employed about 160 native porters because beasts of burden were too dangerous due to tse tse flies.
facts.quote: The expedition initially employed about 160 native porters, as beasts of burden could not be used because of the danger posed by the tse tse fly

facts.statement: Giraffatitan is a genus of sauropod dinosaur, with a name meaning "titanic giraffe".
facts.quote: Giraffatitan (name meaning "titanic giraffe") is a genus of sauropod dinosaur

facts.statement: A partial skeleton known as Skelett Y was found in quarry Y.
facts.quote: A partial skeleton called "Skelett Y" (skeleton Y) was discovered in quarry "Y".

facts.statement: German paleontologist Werner Janensch first described the animal in 1914 as Brachiosaurus brancai based on fossils found between 1909 and 1912.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan brancai was first named and described by German paleontologist Werner Janensch in 1914 as Brachiosaurus brancai, based on several specimens recovered between 1909 and 1912 from the Tendaguru formation.

facts.statement: The animal lived between 145 and 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: It lived from 145 to 150 million years ago, during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic period.

facts.statement: The lectotype specimen is the partial skeleton Skelett SII from Tendaguru.
facts.quote: The lectotype material of Giraffatitan brancai is skeleton "Skelett SII", a partial skeleton from Tendaguru.

facts.statement: The mounted skeleton at the Berlin Natural History Museum is one of the largest and tallest mounted dinosaur skeletons in the world.
facts.quote: A famous specimen of Giraffatitan brancai mounted in the Berlin's Natural History Museum is one of the largest, and in fact the tallest, mounted skeletons in the world, as certified by the Guinness Book of Records.

facts.statement: The name Giraffatitan was elevated to full genus status by George Olshevsky in 1991.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was raised to full genus level by George Olshevsky in 1991, while referring to the vertebral variation.

facts.statement: While Daniel Chure rejected the separation in 2010, most studies have recognized Giraffatitan as a distinct genus since 2012.
facts.quote: The split was rejected by Daniel Chure in 2010, but from 2012 onward most studies recognized the name Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: From 1914 until the 1990s, Giraffatitan was considered the largest known dinosaur and the largest land animal in history.
facts.quote: Between 1914 and the 1990s, Giraffatitan was claimed to be the largest dinosaur known (ignoring the possibly larger but lost Maraapunisaurus) and thus the largest land animal in history.

facts.statement: Most size estimates for the species are based on the Berlin museum mount, which combines authentic bones with reconstructions.
facts.quote: All size estimates for Giraffatitan are based on the skeleton mounted in Berlin, which is partly constructed from authentic bones.

facts.statement: The frequently cited length of 22.46 meters was an addition error by the describer Werner Janensch; the correct length is 22.16 meters.
facts.quote: The often mentioned length of 22.46 m is by Werner Janensch, the German scientist who described Giraffatitan, and was the result of an adding error: the correct number should have been 22.16 m.

facts.statement: Historical mass estimates for the animal have varied widely, ranging from 15 to 78 tonnes.
facts.quote: Mass estimates are more problematic and historically have strongly varied from as little as 15 t to as much as 78 t.

facts.statement: In 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert estimated a weight of 78,258 kg based on a volume measurement of 86.953 cubic meters.
facts.quote: In 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert measured a volume of 86.953 m3. Presuming a density of 0.9, this resulted in a weight of 78,258 kg.

facts.statement: The largest known specimen is HMN XV2, which has a fibula 13% larger than that of the Berlin mount and may have reached 26 meters in length.
facts.quote: HMN SII is not the largest specimen known (an assertion supported by its subadult status) but HMN XV2, represented by a fibula 13% larger than the corresponding material on HMN SII, which might have attained 26 m in length.

facts.statement: A 2020 study estimated the largest specimen to be 25 meters long, 48 tonnes, and 6.8 meters tall at the shoulder.
facts.quote: In 2020, Molina-Perez and Larramnedi estimated the size of the HMN XV2 specimen at 25 m and 48 t, with a shoulder height of 6.8 m.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan was a four-legged, plant-eating sauropod dinosaur characterized by a very long neck and tail.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan was a sauropod, one of a group of four-legged, plant-eating dinosaurs with long necks and tails.

facts.statement: The tail of Giraffatitan accounted for approximately 27.2% of its total body length.
facts.quote: The estimated tail length makes up approximately 27.2% of the total body length.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan possessed a giraffe-like body plan featuring long forelimbs and an exceptionally long neck.
facts.quote: It had a giraffe-like build, with long forelimbs and a very long neck.

facts.statement: The skull of Giraffatitan featured a tall arch in front of the eyes containing bony nares, various openings, and spatulate teeth that resembled chisels.
facts.quote: The skull had a tall arch anterior to the eyes, consisting of the bony nares, a number of other openings, and "spatulate" teeth (resembling chisels).

facts.statement: It is debated whether the distinctive high-crested skull was a true characteristic of the genus Brachiosaurus, as the only known specimens of Brachiosaurus altithorax are now classified as Giraffatitan.
facts.quote: Traditionally, the distinctive high-crested skull was seen as a characteristic of the genus Brachiosaurus, to which Giraffatitan brancai was originally referred; however, it is possible that Brachiosaurus altithorax did not show this feature, since within the traditional Brachiosaurus material it is known only from Tanzanian specimens now assigned to Giraffatitan.

facts.statement: The exact location of the fleshy nostrils in Giraffatitan has been a subject of significant debate, with researchers proposing as many as five possible positions.
facts.quote: The placement of Giraffatitan nostrils has been the source of much debate with Witmer (2001) describing in Science the hypothesized position of the fleshy nostrils in Giraffatitan in as many as five possible locations.

facts.statement: Researchers have hypothesized that Giraffatitan might have possessed a trunk, though this idea is largely discredited due to the lack of narrow-snouted sauropods.
facts.quote: There has also been the hypothesis of various sauropods, such as Giraffatitan, possessing a trunk. The fact that there were no narrow-snouted sauropods (Giraffatitan included) tends to discredit such a hypothesis.

facts.statement: Evidence from tooth wear patterns suggests Giraffatitan did not have a trunk, as the wear indicates biting and tearing plants rather than grinding pre-ripped vegetation.
facts.quote: Stronger evidence for the absence of a trunk is found in the teeth wear of Giraffatitan, which shows the kind of wear that would result from biting and tearing off of plant matter rather than purely grinding, which would be the result of having already ripped the leaves and branches off with a trunk.

facts.statement: Historically, scientists believed the nostrils of Giraffatitan were located on the top of its head.
facts.quote: The nostrils of Giraffatitan, like the huge corresponding nasal openings in its skull, were long thought to be located on the top of the head.

facts.statement: Past theories suggested Giraffatitan used its high nostrils like a snorkel to breathe while submerged in water to support its massive body weight.
facts.quote: In past decades, scientists theorized that the animal used its nostrils like a snorkel, spending most of its time submerged in water in order to support its great mass.

facts.statement: The current scientific consensus is that Giraffatitan was a fully terrestrial animal.
facts.quote: The current consensus view, however, is that Giraffatitan was a fully terrestrial animal.

facts.statement: Studies indicate that water pressure would have prevented Giraffatitan from breathing effectively underwater and that its narrow feet were unsuited for aquatic locomotion.
facts.quote: Studies have demonstrated that water pressure would have prevented the animal from breathing effectively while submerged and that its feet were too narrow for efficient aquatic use.

facts.statement: Research by Lawrence Witmer in 2001 suggests that despite high skull openings, the nostrils of Giraffatitan were located near the snout tip, and the tall crests may have supported a fleshy resonating chamber.
facts.quote: Furthermore, new studies by Lawrence Witmer (2001) show that, while the nasal openings in the skull were placed high above the eyes, the nostrils would still have been close to the tip of the snout (a study which also lends support to the idea that the tall "crests" of brachiosaurs supported some sort of fleshy resonating chamber).

facts.statement: The brain of Giraffatitan measured approximately 300 cm3, which was small relative to its massive body size.
facts.quote: Giraffatitans brain measured about 300 cm3, which, like those of other sauropods, was small compared to its massive body size.

facts.statement: A 2009 study estimated the Encephalization Quotient of Giraffatitan to be between 0.62 and 0.79, depending on the body size estimate used.
facts.quote: A 2009 study calculated its Encephalization Quotient (a rough estimate of possible intelligence) at a low 0.62 or 0.79, depending on the size estimate used.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan possessed a sacral enlargement above the hip, which older sources incorrectly called a "second brain" but is now understood to likely be glycogen bodies.
facts.quote: Like other sauropods, Giraffatitan has a sacral enlargement above the hip which some older sources misleadingly referred to as a "second brain". However, glycogen bodies are a more likely explanation.

facts.statement: In 2001, paleontologist Lawrence M. Witmer argued that the fleshy nostrils of Giraffatitan were located at the front of the bony opening, similar to modern land animals, rather than on top of the head.
facts.quote: The American paleontologist Lawrence M. Witmer rejected this reconstruction in 2001, pointing out that all living vertebrate land animals have their external fleshy nostrils placed at the front of the bony nostril.

facts.statement: Czerkas suggested that the large nasal opening of Giraffatitan accommodated tissue for a keen sense of smell to help locate vegetation.
facts.quote: He suggested that the expanded nasal opening would have made room for tissue related to the animal's ability to smell, which would have helped smell proper vegetation.

facts.statement: Researchers have proposed that Giraffatitan may have possessed a proboscis to aid in feeding, though this hypothesis is disputed by some colleagues who note the facial nerve was not enlarged as in elephants.
facts.quote: It has been proposed that sauropods, including Giraffatitan, may have had proboscises (trunks) based on the position of the bony narial orifice, to increase their upward reach.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan lived in what is now Tanzania during the Late Jurassic period in the Tendaguru Formation.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan lived in what is now Tanzania in the Late Jurassic Tendaguru Formation.

facts.statement: The climate of the Late Jurassic Tendaguru ecosystem was subtropical to tropical, featuring seasonal rains and pronounced dry periods.
facts.quote: The Late Jurassic Tendaguru climate was subtropical to tropical with seasonal rains and pronounced dry periods.

facts.statement: The species G. brancai was originally described by Janensch in 1914.
facts.quote: species_authority: (Janensch, 1914)

facts.statement: Giraffatitan is considered one of the largest animals that ever walked on Earth.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan es uno de los mayores animales que caminó sobre la faz de la Tierra.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan brancai was a four-legged, herbivorous sauropod with a long neck, relatively short tail, and small brain and skull.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan brancai es un saurópodo de cuatro patas, herbívoro, de cuello largo, una cola relativamente corta y un cerebro y cráneo bastante pequeños.

facts.statement: Unlike other sauropods, Giraffatitan had a build similar to modern giraffes, with long front legs compared to the hind legs.
facts.quote: A diferencia de otros saurópodos, tenía una constitución similar a la de las actuales jirafas, con largas patas delanteras , en comparación a las traseras.

facts.statement: Giraffatitan possessed spatulate teeth well-suited for its diet.
facts.quote: Tenía unos dientes espatulados muy adecuados para su dieta.

facts.statement: The skull of Giraffatitan featured many holes, likely to reduce weight, and a characteristic crest.
facts.quote: Su cráneo presenta bastantes agujeros, probablemente para reducir su peso, y una cresta característica.

facts.statement: The first toe of its front feet and the first three toes of its hind feet had claws.
facts.quote: El primer dedo de sus patas delanteras y los tres primeros de sus patas traseras tenían garras.

facts.statement: For decades, Giraffatitan was considered the largest known dinosaur in the world.
facts.quote: Durante décadas, Giraffatitan fue considerado mundialmente como el mayor dinosaurio conocido.

facts.statement: Based on the nearly complete holotype specimen HMN SII housed in the Berlin Natural History Museum, Giraffatitan is estimated to have reached 21.8 to 23 meters in length and 13 meters in height.
facts.quote: Basándose en el espécimen holotipo, HMN SII, conocido por un esqueleto casi completo que se expone en el Museo de Historia Natural de Berlín, Giraffatitan se estima que alcanzó entre 21,8 y 23 metros de longitud y probablemente medía 13 metros de altura hasta la cabeza.

facts.statement: Recent weight estimates based on reconstructed models accounting for air sacs and muscle mass place Giraffatitan between 23.2 and 39.5 tonnes.
facts.quote: Las estimaciones más recientes de su peso, basadas en modelos reconstruidos que toman en cuenta datos modernos de su osteología, como los sacos de aire y una finamente estimada masa muscular, calculan a este saurópodo en el rango de 23,2 a 39,5 toneladas.

facts.statement: Mass estimates for Giraffatitan have historically varied widely, ranging from as low as 15 tonnes to as high as 78 tonnes.
facts.quote: Las estimaciones de masa son más problemáticas e históricamente han variado fuertemente desde tan solo 15 toneladas hasta 78 toneladas.

facts.statement: In 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert estimated a volume of 86.953 cubic meters, which, assuming a density of 0.9, resulted in a weight of 78,258 kilograms.
facts.quote: En 1962, Edwin Harris Colbert midió un volumen de 86.953 m³. Suponiendo una densidad de 0,9, esto resultó en un peso de 78,258 kilogramos.

facts.statement: In 1980, Dale Alan Russell published a much lower weight estimate of 14.8 tonnes by extrapolating from the humerus and femur diameters.
facts.quote: En 1980, Dale Alan Russell publicó un peso mucho menor de 14,8 toneladas extrapolando el diámetro del húmero y el fémur.

facts.statement: Traditionally, the distinctive high-crowned skull was considered a characteristic of the genus Brachiosaurus, to which Giraffatitan brancai was originally referred.
facts.quote: Tradicionalmente, el distintivo cráneo de cresta alta se consideraba una característica del género Brachiosaurus, al que se refería originalmente Giraffatitan brancai.

facts.statement: The location of Giraffatitan's nasal openings has been a subject of much debate, with Witmer describing in 2001 as many as five possible hypothetical positions for the fleshy nasal openings.
facts.quote: La ubicación de las fosas nasales de Giraffatitan ha sido motivo de mucho debate con Witmer en 2001 que describe en Science la posición hipotética de las fosas nasales carnosas de Giraffatitan en tantas como cinco ubicaciones posibles.

facts.statement: A hypothesis has existed that various sauropods, including Giraffatitan, possessed a trunk.
facts.quote: También ha existido la hipótesis de varios saurópodos, como Giraffatitan, tuviesen una trompa.

facts.statement: Evidence for the absence of a trunk in Giraffatitan is found in tooth wear patterns, which show damage consistent with biting and tearing vegetation rather than grinding, as would occur if it had a trunk.
facts.quote: Se encuentra mayor evidencia de la ausencia de una trompa en el desgaste de los dientes de Giraffatitan, que muestra el tipo de desgaste que se produciría al morder y arrancar la materia vegetal en lugar de puramente moler, lo que sería el resultado de haber rasgado las hojas. y se ramifica con su trompa.

facts.statement: The German paleontologist Werner Janensch first named and described the animal in 1914 under the name Brachiosaurus brancai.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan brancai fue nombrado y descrito por primera vez por el paleontólogo alemán Werner Janensch en 1914 como Brachiosaurus brancai

facts.statement: The fossils were recovered between 1909 and 1912 from the Tendaguru Formation.
facts.quote: basado en varios especímenes recuperados entre 1909 y 1912 de la formación Tendaguru

facts.statement: Scientists know the animal from five partial skeletons, including three skulls and numerous fragmentary remains.

facts.statement: The animal lived between 145 and 150 million years ago during the Late Jurassic Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages.

facts.statement: A key difference between the genera is body shape, with Brachiosaurus having a trunk 23% longer and a tail 20 to 25% longer and higher.
facts.quote: Una diferencia importante entre los dos géneros es la forma general del cuerpo, con Brachiosaurus teniendo un tronco 23% más largo y una cola 20 a 25% más larga y también más alta

facts.statement: A mounted specimen at the Museum of Natural History in Berlin is one of the largest and tallest skeletons in the world, certified by the Guinness Book of World Records.
facts.quote: Un famoso espécimen de Giraffatitan brancai montado en el Museo de Historia Natural de Berlín es uno de los esqueletos más grandes y más altos del mundo, como lo certifica el Libro Guinness de los Récords

facts.statement: The genus time range is recorded as Oxfordian to Tithonian, from 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Tithonian (161.5 to 143.1 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus is Brachiosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Brachiosauridae

facts.statement: The animal belongs to the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: The animal's cranial vault, occupied essentially by the brain, had a volume of only 300 cm³.
facts.quote: Su bóveda craneal, espacio ocupado esencialmente por el cerebro, tenía un volumen de solo de 300 cm³

facts.statement: The animal was one of the largest dinosaurs in the Jurassic, living in meadows filled with ferns, bennettites, and horsetails.
facts.quote: Giraffatitan fue uno de los más grandes dinosaurios en el Jurásico, viviendo en praderas llenas de helechos, bennetites y equisetos

facts.statement: It moved and fed among vast forests of conifers, cycads, seed ferns, and ginkgos.
facts.quote: moviéndose y alimentándose entre los vastos bosques de coníferas y cícadas, helechos con semilla y ginkgos
